title: Skin Tests, Targeted Panels and Penicillin Allergy Testing
summary: Learn how a skin prick test is controlled and read, when intradermal testing is used, why allergy testing should follow the history instead of large screening panels, and how a penicillin allergy label is evaluated with major and minor determinants and an observed challenge.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 56 Hits 6 (skin-test thresholds), 12 (indiscriminate panels discouraged) and 16 (penicillin allergy) and Trap 3 (huge allergen panel). Checked against Heinzerling 2013 (European SPT standards), Ansotegui 2020 (WAO), Heffler 2015 (Italian Choosing Wisely list), the CDC 2021 STI treatment guidelines (penicillin allergy section; Workowski 2021) and Jeimy 2020 (Canadian beta-lactam position statement). Corrections and qualifications: the minor determinants are benzylpenicillin, benzylpenicilloate and benzylpenilloate, not “penicillenic acid-protein” (rv-penicillin-minor-determinants); a negative penicillin skin test is followed by an observed oral challenge (rv-penicillin-negative-skin-test); the ≥3 mm prick threshold is measured differently by different standards and the intradermal dilution is 10–1000-fold or more (rv-spt-wheal-method). Not taught as fact: intradermal 1+ = 5–10 mm wheal; “<30% of probable immediate histories are skin-test positive”; repeat IgE to monitor immunotherapy or to stop venom therapy (no open source read in this session states it). The AAAAI Choosing Wisely list page was checked but no longer carries the list.

objectives: Describe how a skin prick test is controlled, timed and read, and when intradermal testing is used.
Explain why allergy tests should be chosen from the clinical history rather than run as large screening panels.
Outline the evaluation of a penicillin allergy label, including the major and minor determinant reagents and the observed oral challenge.

scenes.title: Three allergy requests
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three requests reach the allergy service — (1) a 30-year-old with no current symptoms asks for a “100-allergen IgE panel to see what I’m allergic to”; (2) an inpatient labelled “penicillin allergic” after a childhood rash now needs a penicillin; (3) a skin prick test sheet shows histamine 6 mm, saline 0 mm, cat 4 mm, dog 2 mm. Question token: “Which test, and how is it read?”

cues.text: Three requests arrive. A person with no current symptoms wants a hundred-allergen panel. An inpatient labelled penicillin allergic since a childhood rash now needs penicillin.
And a skin prick test sheet: histamine six millimetres, saline zero, cat four, dog two.
Which test fits each request, and how is each result read?

props.label: Which test, and how is it read?

scenes.title: Prick first, intradermal second
scenes.altText: Schematic forearm with a row of prick sites. Card 1: skin prick test (SPT) — histamine positive control and saline negative control; read at 15–20 minutes; positive = wheal at least 3 mm (European standard: largest wheal diameter; WAO: 3 mm more than the negative control). Card 2: controls — negative control exposes dermographism; histamine control catches antihistamine suppression. Card 3: intradermal test (IDT) — extract diluted about 10- to 1000-fold or more from the prick concentration; more sensitive, less specific; done only after a negative SPT, mainly for venom and drug allergy.

cues.text: The skin prick test is the first-line skin test. Every sheet includes a histamine positive control and a saline negative control, and the sites are read at fifteen to twenty minutes.
A wheal of three millimetres or more is positive. European standards measure the largest wheal diameter; the World Allergy Organization frames it as three millimetres more than the negative control.
The controls protect the reading. A wheal at the saline site signals dermographism; a missing histamine wheal signals suppression, for example by antihistamines.

The intradermal test uses extract diluted roughly ten- to a thousand-fold or more. It is more sensitive but less specific, follows a negative prick test, and is used mainly for venom and drug allergy.

scenes.title: Test to the history, not the menu
scenes.altText: Card “Sensitization is common”: a positive SPT without allergic disease occurs in about 8–30% of people tested with a local aeroallergen panel (WAO); about 25% of the population is sensitized to insect venom, so nonspecific venom screening produces clinically irrelevant results. Card “Not routinely indicated” (WAO): screening without symptoms, nonspecific symptoms, judging immunotherapy effectiveness (may be supportive for venom). Card “Choosing Wisely (Italian allergy society)”: no drug or food allergy tests without a suggestive history; no serological allergy tests (total IgE, specific IgE, component panels) as first-line screening; do not treat a sensitization that does not match symptoms.

cues.text: Sensitization is common. With a local aeroallergen panel, about eight to thirty percent of people have a positive prick test without allergic disease, and about a quarter are sensitized to insect venom.

So the World Allergy Organization does not routinely recommend skin testing to screen people without symptoms, for nonspecific symptoms, or to judge immunotherapy effectiveness, except as support in venom therapy.
An Italian Choosing Wisely list agrees: no drug or food allergy tests without a suggestive history, and no total IgE, specific IgE or component panels as first-line screening.
The harm is a sensitization treated as an allergy: needless diets, avoided drugs, or immunotherapy. Choose the allergens the history points to.

scenes.title: Testing a penicillin label
scenes.altText: Card “The label”: about 10% of the US population reports penicillin allergy, but in studies combining skin testing and oral challenge among people reporting it, the true allergy rate is about 1.5–6.1%. Card “Reagents”: major determinant = benzylpenicilloyl polylysine (Pre-Pen); minor determinants = benzylpenicillin, benzylpenicilloate, benzylpenilloate; prick first, intradermal if prick is negative; no antihistamines for 7 days. Card “Next step”: negative skin test → observed oral amoxicillin challenge (minor-determinant coverage is incomplete); positive → avoid β-lactams, desensitize if penicillin is the only option. Canadian position: low-risk histories may go straight to an observed challenge. Hook answers.

cues.text: About ten percent of people report a penicillin allergy, yet when those patients have skin testing and oral challenge, only about one and a half to six percent prove truly allergic.

The skin test uses the major determinant, benzylpenicilloyl polylysine, plus minor determinants: benzylpenicillin, benzylpenicilloate and benzylpenilloate. Prick first, intradermal if the prick is negative, and no antihistamines for seven days.

A negative skin test is followed by an observed oral amoxicillin challenge, because the minor determinants are not fully covered. A positive test means avoiding beta-lactams, or desensitization if penicillin is the only option.
Back to the hook. No hundred-allergen panel without a history. The penicillin label gets a structured evaluation. And cat at four millimetres is positive; dog at two is not.

lines: 3 Cat 4 mm positive · dog 2 mm negative

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A large panel shows what they are allergic to” (✓ positives may be sensitization only; test to the history); “The minor determinant is penicillenic acid” (✓ CDC lists benzylpenicillin, benzylpenicilloate and benzylpenilloate; WAO lists benzylpenicillin and benzylpenilloate); “A negative penicillin skin test ends the work-up” (✓ CDC follows it with an observed oral amoxicillin challenge).

cues.text: Trap one: a big panel shows what the patient is allergic to. No: it finds sensitizations, many clinically irrelevant. Test to the history.
Trap two: the minor determinant is penicillenic acid. The minor-determinant reagents in current guidance are benzylpenicillin, benzylpenicilloate and benzylpenilloate.
Trap three: a negative penicillin skin test ends the work-up. No: an observed oral amoxicillin challenge confirms it.

scenes.title: Map, flashlight, test drive
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The HISTORY is the map, the SKIN TEST is the flashlight, the CHALLENGE is the test drive. Shine the light only where the map points, call it lit at 3 mm, and before you clear a penicillin label, take the test drive.” Tokens: map = history · flashlight = SPT ≥3 mm · test drive = observed challenge. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the history is the map, the skin test is the flashlight, the challenge is the test drive. Shine the light only where the map points, call it lit at three millimetres, and take the test drive before clearing a penicillin label.

Where it breaks: wheal cut-offs and measurement rules vary by device and guideline; a positive test without symptoms can predict later allergy; and low-risk penicillin histories may skip skin testing and go straight to an observed challenge.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “SPT with controls · read 15–20 min · wheal ≥3 mm positive · intradermal only after a negative prick”, “Test to the history · penicillin label: major + minor determinants, then observed challenge”.

cues.text: Read a skin prick test against its controls and call a wheal of three millimetres or more positive, test only for allergens the history points to, and evaluate a penicillin label with major and minor determinant skin tests followed by an observed oral challenge when they are negative.

props.label: Controls · 15–20 min · wheal ≥ 3 mm · intradermal after negative prick
Test to the history · penicillin: major + minor, then challenge

explanation.what: Plain language: a skin test puts a tiny amount of allergen into the skin and looks for a raised bump after about a quarter of an hour; it only means something when the control spots behave and when the allergen was chosen because of the patient’s story. Most people with a penicillin-allergy label can take penicillin, and a structured test can show this. Scientific terms: skin prick test (SPT), wheal, positive (histamine) and negative (saline) controls, dermographism, intradermal test (IDT), sensitization, major determinant (benzylpenicilloyl polylysine), minor determinants (benzylpenicillin, benzylpenicilloate, benzylpenilloate), graded or observed oral challenge, desensitization.
explanation.why: IgE sensitization is common and often clinically irrelevant, so untargeted testing generates positives that lead to needless diets, avoided drugs or unnecessary immunotherapy. Penicillin-allergy labels are usually wrong and push patients onto less effective, costlier antibiotics; skin testing with determinant reagents, followed by challenge, removes most labels safely.
explanation.measure: SPT: histamine and saline controls; read at 15–20 min; positive wheal ≥3 mm (largest diameter in the European standard; 3 mm above the negative control in WAO wording). IDT: extract 10–1000-fold or more diluted; after a negative SPT; mainly venom and drugs. Penicillin: ~10% report allergy, ~1.5–6.1% truly allergic in studies with skin test plus challenge; PPL major determinant plus minor determinants; prick then intradermal; no antihistamines for 7 days; negative → observed oral amoxicillin challenge; positive → avoid β-lactams or desensitize.
explanation.differs: Sensitization (positive test) vs clinical allergy (positive test plus matching symptoms); prick vs intradermal (more sensitive, less specific, more dilute); major vs minor penicillin determinants; skin test plus challenge vs direct challenge for low-risk histories.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: read a prick test sheet with controls, choose the appropriate response to a request for a large screening panel, identify a minor determinant reagent, or name the step after a negative penicillin skin test.

mnemonic.text: The HISTORY is the map, the SKIN TEST is the flashlight, the CHALLENGE is the test drive. Shine the light only where the map points, call it lit at 3 mm, and before you clear a penicillin label, take the test drive.
mnemonic.explanation: History chooses the allergens; SPT ≥3 mm is positive; an observed challenge confirms a negative penicillin work-up.
mnemonic.limitation: Wheal cut-offs and measurement rules vary by device and guideline; a positive test in a symptom-free person can predict later allergy; low-risk penicillin histories may go straight to an observed challenge without skin testing.

Penicillin testing details follow US (CDC) and Canadian guidance; reagent availability differs between countries.

questions.stem: A skin prick test is read at 15 minutes: histamine control 6 mm, saline control 0 mm, cat 4 mm, dog 2 mm. How should the cat and dog results be interpreted?

options.rationale: Correct. With valid controls, a wheal of at least 3 mm (here 4 mm above a 0 mm negative control) is positive; 2 mm is below the threshold.

options.text: Both positive, because any wheal counts
options.rationale: Incorrect. A wheal must reach at least 3 mm to be called positive.

options.text: Both negative, because they are smaller than the histamine wheal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Allergen wheals are not judged against the size of the histamine wheal; histamine only shows the skin can respond.

options.text: The test is invalid because the saline control is 0 mm
options.rationale: Incorrect. A 0 mm saline control is the expected result; a wheal there would suggest dermographism.

questions.stem: Which reagent is used as a MINOR determinant in penicillin skin testing?

options.rationale: Correct. CDC 2021 lists benzylpenicillin, benzylpenicilloate and benzylpenilloate as minor determinants; WAO 2020 lists benzylpenicillin and benzylpenilloate.
Incorrect. This is the major determinant reagent (Pre-Pen).
Incorrect. Histamine is the positive control, not a penicillin determinant.
Incorrect. CDC states aged penicillin is not an adequate source of minor determinants; penicillin G should be fresh or fresh-frozen.

questions.stem: A healthy adult with no allergic symptoms asks the laboratory for a large specific-IgE panel “to see what I’m allergic to.” Which response best follows current guidance?

options.text: Explain that testing should be guided by a suggestive history, because screening panels detect sensitizations that are often clinically irrelevant
options.rationale: Correct. WAO does not routinely recommend testing to screen people without symptoms, and the Italian Choosing Wisely list advises against IgE panels as first-line screening.

options.text: Run the panel and label every positive allergen as an allergy
options.rationale: Incorrect. A positive test without matching symptoms shows sensitization only.

options.text: Measure total IgE instead, since a normal value excludes allergy
options.rationale: Incorrect. Total IgE neither proves nor excludes allergy and is not a screening test for it.

options.text: Order food-specific IgG4 testing as a cheaper alternative
options.rationale: Incorrect. Food IgG or IgG4 panels are unproven for diagnosing allergy.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 56 Hit 16 names the penicillin minor determinant as “penicillenic acid-protein”. CDC 2021 (Workowski) lists the minor-determinant reagents as benzylpenicillin, benzylpenicilloate and benzylpenilloate, and WAO 2020 (Ansotegui) as benzylpenicillin and benzylpenilloate; neither names penicillenic acid; the lesson teaches the source list (register flag rv-penicillin-minor-determinants).

Ch. 56 Hit 16 says immediate reactions are rare after negative skin tests. CDC 2021 adds that because minor-determinant coverage is incomplete, a negative skin test is followed by an observed oral amoxicillin challenge; Jeimy 2020 notes the 93% NPV comes from a 1971 adult study and sensitivity can be low in children (register flag rv-penicillin-negative-skin-test).

Ch. 56 Hit 6 gives “≥3 mm mean wheal” and prick extracts “up to 1000-fold” more concentrated. The European standard (Heinzerling 2013) measures the largest wheal diameter; WAO 2020 defines positive as 3 mm above the negative control, describes mean-diameter recording options and notes device-specific thresholds; intradermal extracts are 1:10–1:1000 (Heinzerling) or 10–1000-fold or more (WAO) dilute, so “up to 1000-fold” is not a strict ceiling (register flag rv-spt-wheal-method).
Penicillin skin-test reagents and the challenge pathway follow US (CDC) and Canadian guidance; reagent availability differs between countries and Philippine practice guidance is not covered.
